figures.caption: Table 1: Experiment 1: RMRNN versus RNN baseline over 1,000 replications. Regime I = i.i.d. inputs; Regime II = AR(1) inputs. RMRNN reduces Q̂ by 43% (Regime I) and 58% (Regime II) with task-loss increases of approximately 7%.

Table 4: Experiment 4 (Panel A and Panel B): sensitivity to hidden dimension p and sequence length T ; i.i.d. task, λ0 = 0.1, 1,000 replications. Q̂ scales approximately linearly with T and decreases slowly with p.

Table 5: Experiment 4: spectral normalisation versus backward-coherence regularisation (p = 32, T = 100, 1,000 replications). rT = ∑ t ∥δt∥ is an empirical backward-defect tail proxy. Spectral normalisation reduces hidden-state variance; backward coherence halves Q̂ and rT ; the combined model achieves all simultaneously.

Table 6: Experiment 5: stopping-time statistics and coverage (i.i.d. scenario, 1,000 replications). Coverage = proportion of replications in which τδ < Tmax. RMRNN stops 36–38% earlier and achieves higher coverage at each tolerance level.

Figure 1: Experiment 6: echo-state forgetting. Left : normalised mean discrepancy ēt/ē1 (log scale); dashed lines show the theoretical upper bound ρt−1. Right : raw ēt (log scale); dotted lines show the fitted geometric α̂t for ρ = 0.9. For ρ ∈ {0.3, 0.5} the curve drops below the 2% noise floor within 4 steps. AR(1) input with ϕ = 0.7; 10 replications, 500 test trajectories.

Figure 2: Experiment 7: Left : simultaneous coverage vs calibration constant C for the increment-sum tube Rt (solid, direct) and defect-tail proxy Q̂t (dashed); horizontal dotted line marks 95%. Centre: median ratio ∥ht − hT∥/Q̂t over time. Right : median inflation factor Rt/∥ht − hT∥ over time; values ≫ 1 show that Rt is a loose bound in practice. Rt achieves 100% simultaneous coverage at C = 1 (triangle inequality) but with median inflation 17–30; Q̂t needs only C∗ = 1.15. AR(1) and i.i.d. inputs; T = 60, B = 1,000, 5 reps.

Table 9: PhysioNet 2012 ICU Challenge: RMRNN versus baselines. Mean (SD) over 20× 3 = 60 fold observations. Q̂= empirical quasi-martingale total; τ̄0.05 = mean stopping time at tolerance δ = 0.05 (hours into the 48-h stay at which ∥ht − ht+1∥ ≤ 0.05 first).

Table 10: FRED-MD macroeconomic study: RMRNN versus baselines. Mean (SD) over 20 expanding-window seeds. Task: 1-month-ahead INDPRO growth. Q̂= empirical quasi-martingale total; τ̄0.05 = mean stopping time (months within the 60-month window at which ∥ht − ht+1∥ ≤ 0.05 first).

Figure 3: FRED-MD: RMRNN empirical quasi-martingale total Q̂t over rolling 60-month evaluation windows (January 1960–November 2024), with NBER recession periods shaded. Q̂t rises at the onset of each recession and declines during subsequent recoveries, confirming it as a real-time diagnostic of concept drift consistent with Proposition 3.16.

Table 11: UCI HAR activity recognition: RMRNN versus baselines. Mean (SD) over 20× 3 = 60 fold observations. Q̂= empirical quasi-martingale total; τ̄0.05 = mean stopping time (steps within the 128-step window at which ∥ht − ht+1∥ ≤ 0.05 first).

Figure 4: UCI HAR: mean tracking-error E[∥ht−mnew∥] step-by-step after an activity transition, averaged across all transition pairs. t = 0 is the final hidden state of the oldactivity window (before any new-activity input); t = 1, . . . , 128 are time steps within the first new-activity window. Left: linear scale; right: log scale with log-linear fit (dotted), exposing the empirical geometric rate ρ̂ < 1. RMRNN (solid) shows steeper, more regular decay than the RNN baseline (dashed), consistent with the stronger contraction guaranteed by the backward-coherence penalty (Proposition 3.16).
